chunks: Ahmad ibn A'idh narrated from Abu Salamah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding two slave men who were authorized to buy and sell with the wealth of their masters. A dispute arose between them, and they fought. Each ran to the master of the other. They were equal in strength. One purchased the other from his master, and the other did the same, purchasing his opponent from his master. Then each of them grabbed the collar of the other, saying, 'You are my slave; I have purchased you.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'They should be judged based on the point where they separated. The path should be measured, and whichever one was closer to his master, he is considered to have reached first and thus has precedence over the one farther away. But if both distances are equal, they are returned to their respective masters.'

key_terms.تَلْبِيب: collar or neck area (grabbing by the collar)

ai.seo_question: How is ownership determined when two slaves simultaneously purchase each other from their masters?
ai.summary: This ruling from *Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih* illustrates the application of *al-‘Adl* (justice) and *al-Qasam* (proportionality) in resolving ambiguous property disputes among *mukatab* or authorized slaves. The Imam’s criterion of measuring the path (*idra’ al-tariq*) serves as a practical legal mechanism to determine precedence when simultaneous actions occur, ensuring that the outcome reflects the actual effort and proximity of the parties involved. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on objective, measurable criteria (*qarain*) to resolve *ikhtilaf* (disagreement) in commercial and personal status matters.
